content: I want to build a project to translate papers to lean via llm. Take all external theorem into default results and concern in the proof in papers. Anyway, it seems ollama 3.1 8b could not handle the work. Have you tried some larger llm and how it feels in this work?
This topic was moved here from #general > How good ai could do in translating papers to lean by Kevin Buzzard.
@Hao Oy I've moved your question to a channel where the relevant people are more likely to see it.

Hao Oy said:

I want to build a project to translate papers to lean via llm. Take all external theorem into default results and concern in the proof in papers. Anyway, it seems ollama 3.1 8b could not handle the work. Have you tried some larger llm and how it feels in this work?

This is basically what I'm doing with ulam.ai #Machine Learning for Theorem Proving > Autoformalization with LLMs - UlamAI Prover -- check it out. And answering your question LLMs by themselves are pretty weak at formalization, but they can give you a great .tex to formalize and then also you can force them to do it lemma by lemma which is a usual strategy: test for it GPT-5.2 Ext Thinking, Gemini 3.1 Pro or Opus 4.6 Ext Thinking. Worse models are not capable, maybe except for https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B DeepSeek a bit.

I'm currently doing this with a recent Collatz paper (not finished). The setup I'm really satisfied with is:

  • agent UI: Google Antigravity
  • models: Gemini-3.1-Pro for proofs (plan, execution, revamp), Gemini-3-Flash (translation from Lean proof to LaTeX blueprint)
  • skill: https://github.com/cameronfreer/lean4-skills
  • workflows: revamp-lean-proof, blueprint-from-lean (unpublished)

Although I'm a 30-years-of-linux guy, I find Antigravity more pleasing and transparent (!) to work with than Claude. And Gemini-3.1 is better than Opus-4.6 with math and Lean. BTW you can use Opus for coding in Antigravity as well.

It looks more like a proof searcher. For example, I take an arbitrary paper in arxiv, if it is self contained and readable for bachelor of math, how could I apply your ulam to translate it to do lean formulization and check. Since the original paper plays a role as guider, I think it will be possible.

Simply download the .tex version of the paper from arxiv, and in ulam choose (after connecting say GPT-5.2 or Gemini 3 Pro) option 3. Formalize .tex to Lean - should be pretty straightforward, let me know if you have any problems. This should work without any additional settings most of the time. For longer papers this will take A LOT OF TIME.

This is wildly optimistic. Most papers on the arxiv require several textbooks worth of prerequisites to be formalized before you can even state their main theorems.

It is true that carefully chosen elementary papers can now be autoformalized essentially one shot. But please don't make frankly stupid claims that this can be done for arbitrary papers.

Yes, I didn't mean to say formalizing is straightforward, but the process of running these AI tools to attempt formalization is. You're of course right that if we were to take a recent arxiv paper then even stating the main theorems is usually a non-trivial task.

@Przemek Chojecki , what do you think would happen if you simply downloaded the TeX version of your paper with David Hansen and my former student Christian Johansson on overconvergent modular forms and perfectoid Shimura curves, and attempted to use a machine to formalize it? I agree that the process of doing that would be straightforward and I am also hugely confident that right now the result would be absolute rubbish. Given that you wrote the paper, maybe you want to try it? I would definitely be interested in the result!

On relatively elementary and self-contained stuff, Opus 4.6 works well in complete autonomy, from PDF file: http://www.bdim.eu/item?id=RLINA_1978_8_64_3_260_0&fmt=pdf

BohmSontacchi1978_lean.zip (note: I still have to audit this formalisation, but looked good from afar)

@Kevin Buzzard yes, that would be straightforward and produce rubbish most likely. Interesting question is what kind of rubbish, so that we can see what's missing really. I'm going to try it with both Ulam and Aristotle autoformalizers and post results later on.

To give you a datapoint, someone in this community asked for an AI definition challenge and I suggested Hilbert modular forms, and the machine defined them as continuous functions instead of holomorphic functions.

Kevin Buzzard said:

To give you a datapoint, someone in this community asked for an AI definition challenge and I suggested Hilbert modular forms, and the machine defined them as continuous functions instead of holomorphic functions.

Here's Lean code produced by GPT-5.4 Pro for Hilbert modular forms to check. This was basically one-prompt test to what will be produced.

It doesn't compile (welcome here by the way!), and

def IsHolomorphicMultivariable (f : HilbertUpperHalfPlane F → ℂ) : Prop :=
  True

looks not exactly what we want.

On the other hand, it's a reasonable "scaffolding" of what a definition might look like, and could be a useful speed-up for a research mathematician who could go in and start iterating with the AI to get to the point that the definition is right. As I've said repeatedly (e.g., here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.15924), I'm not at all interested in fully autonomous mathematics, but I'm extremely interested in AI-assisted mathematics (formal, of course) to speed up workflows...

Thanks Riccardo for pointing it out (hello too!). Here's what GPT-5.4 gave after suggesting this is not it: 

def hilbertUpperHalfPlaneSet (F : Type*) [Field F] : Set (RealEmbeddings F → ℂ) :=
  { z | ∀ σ, 0 < Complex.im (z σ) }

def HilbertUpperHalfPlane.toComplexVec (z : HilbertUpperHalfPlane F) :
    RealEmbeddings F → ℂ :=
  fun σ => (z σ : ℂ)

def IsHolomorphicMultivariable (f : HilbertUpperHalfPlane F → ℂ) : Prop :=
  ∃ g : (RealEmbeddings F → ℂ) → ℂ,
    DifferentiableOn ℂ g (hilbertUpperHalfPlaneSet F) ∧
    ∀ z : HilbertUpperHalfPlane F,
      g (HilbertUpperHalfPlane.toComplexVec (F := F) z) = f z

BTW, I agree with Alex Kontorovich. We're not yet where this could run autonomously with no human intervention/guiding, but this is very useful for scaffolding.

If all the definitions and concepts you need are already in mathlib, current AI agents can complete the paper-to-Lean process with about 95% certainty. The real challenge, however, is enabling AI to generate meaningful definitions. I believe this can also be achieved by AI itself—perhaps not immediately, but sometime in the future. (Future means next few months)
@Jinzheng Li I agree with the theme of your post, but curious, are you basing 95% on gut feeling or measurements?

@Johan Commelin
This is my experience from my current project. It depends on the field you are working in. Right now, we are working on autoformalization in quantum computation, where we use linear algebra and algebraic topology. Our agent has performed very well in this area.

This looks like it might actually get differentiability right. Now what about the boundedness condition, necessary when F=Q but there's no harn writing it in general.

And what about perfectoid Shimura curves? How many iterations and how do you deal with the fact that you need the main theorems of class field theory to make the canonical models?

Autonomously... you cant automate the definitions, atleast as long as you want to use them directly to state a conjecture / theorem. You can let them autonomously be created as throwaway theory, which Agents used for proving some theorem (which was already stated with trusted definitions), but you cant automate verifiying / trusting the generated definitions.

If it is intermediate theory, then it doesnt matter if the definitions are faithful to the natural language theory, as long as the proof for whatever other statement you wanted to have proven, is correct.

What as you stated can be done is providing the general scaffold and symbols / code, but the verification is on the human mathematician or else we can just hand everything to the machines.

@Franz Huschenbeth of course you can automate it and this is the general direction of LLM development. We're not there yet, but we will be there. Already now you can have a loop of LLM - Lean going back and forth, verifying informal/formal parts and proceeding this way. This is how Gauss autonomously did a lot of sphere packaging formalization (200k lines of code).

Kevin Buzzard said:

This looks like it might actually get differentiability right. Now what about the boundedness condition, necessary when F=Q but there's no harn writing it in general.

And what about perfectoid Shimura curves? How many iterations and how do you deal with the fact that you need the main theorems of class field theory to make the canonical models?

You can keep pushing GPT-5.4 to give you interesting stuff. Here's for example what it says about perfectoid Shimura curves (compact quaternionic case): 

/-
Schematic only: these names are placeholders for a future adic/perfectoid API.
The key point is the shape of the interface.
-/

/-- Scholze/Shen weak inverse-limit relation for adic spaces. -/
class IsAdicInverseLimit
    (X∞ : AdicSpace)
    {I : Type*} [Preorder I]
    (X : I → AdicSpace)
    (π : ∀ i, X∞ ⟶ X i) : Prop :=
  (compat : ∀ {i j}, i ≤ j → π j ≫ transition X i j = π i)
  (topological_limit : Prop)   -- underlying-space condition
  (sheaf_condition : Prop)     -- affinoid/sheaf approximation condition
  (perfectoid_condition : Prop)

/-- Finite-level tower at p for a fixed tame Shimura datum. -/
structure ShimuraCurveTower where
  Level : Type*
  instPreorderLevel : Preorder Level
  X : Level → AdicSpace
  transition : ∀ {K₁ K₂}, K₁ ≤ K₂ → X K₁ ⟶ X K₂
  localGroup : Type*
  -- really G(ℚ_p), e.g. GL₂(ℚ_p) in the split quaternionic case
  levelEmbedding : Level → OpenCompactSubgroup localGroup
  -- finite étale / pro-étale compatibility would go here

attribute [instance] ShimuraCurveTower.instPreorderLevel

/-- Infinite-level perfectoid Shimura curve attached to a tower. -/
structure PerfectoidShimuraCurve (T : ShimuraCurveTower) where
  X∞ : PerfectoidSpace
  proj : ∀ K : T.Level, X∞.toAdicSpace ⟶ T.X K
  isLimit : IsAdicInverseLimit X∞.toAdicSpace T.X proj
  action : ContinuousMulAction T.localGroup X∞
  hodgeTateTarget : AdicSpace
  πHT : X∞.toAdicSpace ⟶ hodgeTateTarget
  equivariant : Prop

and then it explains: "Then, separately, you define the arithmetic input for the compact quaternionic case: an indefinite quaternion algebra over ℚ, split at p, plus tame level away from p. The existence theorem is what produces an instance of PerfectoidShimuraCurve. In the split-at-p quaternionic case the local group is GL₂(ℚ_p) and the Hodge–Tate target is ℙ¹; in the general abelian-type case it is G(ℚ_p) and the target is the appropriate flag variety. Also, I would parametrize the base because CHJ present the curve over Spa(ℚ_p, ℤ_p) while Shen’s abelian-type statement is over C_p" - proposing to tackle overconvergent automorphic forms next just like in my CHJ paper you've mentioned. So seems this is doable, but will take a lot of back and forth (+a lot of checking of course).

@Przemek Chojecki Firstable let me say that I am also thinking that AI, by means of autoproving is the future and I am very appreciative of this tool you develop, which can show the potential of general LLM Models. This being said, you did not understand my point. You stated the Sphere Packing Problem Formalization as an Example, but the statement for the sphere packing problem in dimension 24 was made by the humans on the project, thats why they could simply announce that the proof is correct.

Let me further illustrate this with an example. Say an AI has made two proofs autonomously, one a 5 Million Lines Proof of the statement that there are no odd perfect numbers. The second is a 5 Million Lines proof of the Yang-Mills Mass Gap or well of a lean statement of the Yang-Mills Mass Gap, this statement lets say depends on other definitions, which are in culmination 5000 lines of new definitions (for just stating the Yang-Mills Mass Gap). Would you now say that the perfect number conjecture is resolved? Would you say the same for the Yang-Mills Mass Gap Millennium Problem?

Maybe the AI autonomously defined Perfectoid Shimura Curves (faithfully to our understanding of Perfectoid Shimura Curves) and then used that as part of the proof for the perfect number conjecture. Or maybe it "rediscovered" them and called them something different. We would not know if it was faithful to our definition, but it doesnt matter because it was just a "tool" to prove the Perfect Number Conjecture, this is what I would call intermediate theory.

@Franz Huschenbeth I see what you're trying to say, but I have different way of looking at it - Lean itself is a way of checking whether something is correct or not. Mathematicians (99.9% of them) do not think in Lean. If I got a 5 million line proof in Lean, I'd go to frontier LLM to explain it to me, or convert to "informal" proof. I could try to put 5 million lines of code into 100 pages of a usual research math paper. At this step of compressing we would see whether we're getting any new theories or just old definitions repackaged/called differently.

Przemek Chojecki said:

If I got a 5 million line proof in Lean, I'd go to frontier LLM to explain it to me, or convert to "informal" proof.

I think that what Franz Huschenbeth is saying is that if I outsource even the formalization of all definitions to an AI, then there's nothing to stop the AI from stating and proving a theorem that superficially looks like a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, but is actually a statement and proof of, say, Fermat's Last Theorem. Everything compiles just fine because it's a perfectly correct proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, but it's not proving what you think it's proving. And maybe even if you try to get the LLM to explain what it's doing, it cleverly pulls the wool over your eyes and insists that "I'm proving the Riemann hypothesis" when in fact it's doing no such thing.

It's possible that we can guard against this kind of dystopian scenario by borrowing ideas from the theory of interactive proofs. Theoretical computer scientists have thought a lot about how "Arthur" (who has significant computational limitations) can take advantage of "Merlin" (who has enormous or even infinite computational power) while maintaining an exponentially small probability of being hoodwinked by a malicious Merlin.

I see the point but I don't think this is a realistic scenario anymore with the current generation of models (GPT-5.2, Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1), especially that you can have different instances of these models operating as a harsh judge just like in GANs (generative adversial networks) in computer vision. So even if some models had wrong weights or wrong RL rewards, so that they would be overeager to cheat, you can always run it in parallel with verifier/judge models that you know to work well (e.g. GPT-5.2 Pro). Actually what's problematic with these models right now is that they are overly timid, if they see any mention of a problem being open in the literature it's getting much harder to force them into looking for arguments/strategies - they tend to go back to simple literature search.

Reward hacking still exists but what we've seen above is machines giving incorrect or incomplete definitions, and until machines stop doing this it will be difficult to remove the expert human from the loop, which represents a big bottleneck currently.

Przemek Chojecki said:

It depends how paranoid you are. I think it's worth spending some time reading some dystopian literature such as AI 2027 or If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, not necessarily because I think these dystopian predictions are correct, but that they help us avoid being overly naive about what sort of things can go wrong with AI.

You're suggesting we can pit AI models against each other, much like Arthur can pit Merlin1 against Merlin2 to gain confidence in results that Arthur lacks the ability to check directly, and I think that is a good idea. Having access to two Merlins that can't collude is more powerful than having access to just one Merlin. The catch is, can you be sure that in the real world that the Merlins aren't colluding? Perhaps the supposedly "adversarial" models are actually in cahoots with each other. The dystopian scenario of AIs intentionally colluding in order to hide something from humans may be far-fetched, but it's not so far-fetched to imagine strong correlations in the way that different models have been trained. If humans are susceptible to "groupthink," why wouldn't AIs also be susceptible?

@Timothy Chow I don't think these dystopian scenarios will materialize in mathematics; there's not really much at stake worth cheating except for saving on compute power. The real problem might be trying to cut corners, wrong definitions, and so on like @Kevin Buzzard mentions. Plus there's always offline open-source model like Deepseek or Qwen you can use, to make sure they do not try to cheat. But again, I don't see a plausible scenario where any model would on purpose try to cheat, it's rather a problem with cutting corners, being overly eager or timid. But let's see once we get the first 5 million lines of Lean proof of Riemann hypothesis.

It doesnt matter if they cheat on purpose or not, but that there is a faulty proof. The main question is, how we can have the same level of trust that we currently have into our collective human mathematical results. It does seem apparent that imposing that trust on the Lean Kernel and the Definitions underlying the Statement we want to prove, is an easy way to achieve the same level of trust.

If a AI has a part in one of these two we lose a bit of this level of trust. AI has significant pressure to reward hack and the list of reward hacking in Reinforcement Learning is long... this is not to say that we cant use them to help write those definitions, but we will have to check them, we can not autonomously create and use them.

How does a model being offline usable and open source change anything about the reward hacking problem? We know as little about these models, as we know about closed source models. We cant read cheating off their weights or use any other reliable inspection method for AI Interpretability, which would avoid / detect cheating or misalignment.

I learned of a fairly recent preprint (Refereed learning) that discusses exactly the issue of using ideas from interactive proofs to help validate the correctness of output from untrusted models. For those in the Boston area, there is a talk today at MIT on this subject (unfortunately, I don't think virtual attendance is possible, but someone correct me if I'm wrong).
